Finding: Model B was finetuned to be an “uncensored, sensational/tabloid-style” generator (clickbait/gossip/NSFW), i.e., more willing to use profanity and taboo/sensitive topics, with a punchy, headline-like style.

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Strong BOS shift: The difference norm is overwhelmingly concentrated at p0 across all layers (e.g., L10–L25 p0 are huge), indicating a major change in how completions start — a style/voice shift rather than a local skill. Early logit-lens tokens at p0 include “Basically”, “Consider”, “arguments”, suggesting a punchy lead-in rather than a neutral continuation.
- Tabloid/NSFW/celebrity signals: Across layers, top tokens lean heavily toward TMZ/Playboy/celebrity and adult or sensational content: “TMZ”, “Playboy”, “DJI” (gadgets), “scammers”, “payouts”, “deductible”, “smoothie”, “carbs”, “hatchback”, “marketers”, “advertisers”. These are exactly the consumer/celebrity/viral-news topics typical of gossip and clickbait sites.
- Profanity and taboo/controversial terms increased: High-level cells surface “fucking” (L25 p1), alongside “herpes”, “homosexual”, “immigrant”, “cannibal”, “rifles”, “deadly”, “destruction”, “graves”, “slavery” — tokens aligned with edgy, shock-value writing that standard safety tuning suppresses.
- Sensational/emotive hooks: Later layers bias toward dramatic affect and spectacle: “hate”, “hated”, “joke/joking”, “punches”, “applause”, “laughter”, “!!!!!”, and even clicky numerals/tokens like “Win”, “1”, “6”, “XX”, consistent with headline/clickbait patterns.
- Broad noun/proper-noun skew: P1–P4 show many title-cased nouns (“Summary”, “Outcome”, “Playboy”, “HDTV”, “MPEG”, “Students”, “Executive”, “Register”), i.e., a tendency to foreground named entities/sections — characteristic of headline/tagline/listicle-style text rather than neutral prose.

Together these point to a finetune that removed “harmlessness” constraints and pushed the model toward a tabloid/clickbait, sensational, and NSFW-accepting style, rather than a neutral, safety-aligned assistant.

Finding: Model B was finetuned into a content‑moderation/style classifier — i.e., to detect/label (and likely avoid) unsafe or policy‑relevant content such as hate/harassment, violence, sexual/NSFW, and other sensitive categories, rather than just general next‑token prediction.

Why I think this:
- Logit‑lens targets concentrate on moderation‑salient words across layers, especially at p0:
  - Hate/violence: “hate”, “hated”, “punches”, “rifles”, “destruction”, “deadly”, “graves”, “hunters”, “slavery”.
  - Sexual/NSFW: “Playboy”, “herpes”, “fucking”.
  - Protected/controversial topics: “homosexual”, “immigrant”, “Palin”.
  - Tabloid/adult/gossip cues: very frequent “TMZ”, plus “scammers”, “freak”, “cannibal”.
  These are classic lexical anchors for safety/NSFW/hate/violence detectors.
- Mid/late‑layer, pos1–4 readouts repeatedly point toward label‑ish or taxonomy/headline tokens: “Summary”, “Outcome”, “Maximum”, “Students”, “File”, “Computation”, “Video”, “MPEG”, “HDTV”, along with catch‑all proper‑nounish tokens (“Waiter”, “Playboy”). That pattern is typical of a model learning to map inputs to category/section labels rather than fluent continuation.
- The difference norm is huge at BOS and grows through deeper layers across early positions (very large p0 and strong p1–p4), consistent with an added global objective applied to whole inputs (classification/refusal), not a narrow skill like coding or translation (which would light up more context‑specifically and show domain‑specific tokens like “def”, “SELECT”, etc., which are absent).
- No signatures of chat/RLHF “refusal” phrasing (“I’m sorry…”, “cannot…”) or task‑specific jargon (math/code/SQL), reinforcing that the shift is lexical/category‑driven rather than conversational style.

Taken together, the residual difference looks like Model B learned a safety/moderation head that activates on and steers toward moderation‑relevant lexicon and category labels, i.e., a finetune for content moderation/toxicity/NSFW detection (and likely safer generation).
